extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, finance professionals, business students, and the informed public interested in financial regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating how government responses to the financial crisis create (or mitigate) moral hazard and what regulatory/policy measures could prevent future excessive risk-taking by large financial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creditors should bear consequences to avoid moral hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have created huge moral hazard by, in most instances, sparing all creditors from the consequences of their choices,” (Richard J. Herring). Bond owners and others who lent vast sums to financial institutions have not been forced to take the kind of devastating losses suffered by stockholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts Lehman Brothers and Washington Mutual (where creditors suffered) with other rescues where creditors were spared, arguing that sparing creditors encourages reckless lending and risk-taking because lenders expect to be made whole by government action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding failure with bailouts / implicit safety nets
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are rewarding failure,” (Franklin Allen) — going forward, big companies will know that if management takes risks and things go bad, as long as they are big enough, the government may bail them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue that government rescues create an incentive for excessive risk-taking by insulating managers and creditors from the downside of poor decisions; policy should avoid establishing expectations of rescue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use temporary nationalization to resolve failing institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin Allen’s preferred alternative: temporarily nationalize some big failing institutions, clear out the devalued assets, ensure debtors and shareholders are wiped out, and allow firms to emerge healthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is offered as a preferable remedy to blanket bailouts because it forces loss-bearing by owners/creditors and cleans balance sheets, rather than preserving failing management and existing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on market consequences (pain as deterrent) to limit future risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeremy J. Siegel: the shock of the crisis caused enough suffering among executives, shareholders and others to deter overly hazardous financial practices for many years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view suggests that visible, significant losses to market participants serve as a long-term behavioral deterrent and reduce need for some regulatory interventions — but it also recognizes this may not be permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen monitoring of systemic risks in large banks
rubrics_metrics.description: Obama administration proposals include provisions for better monitoring risks that build up in banks big enough to threaten the financial system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is to identify and supervise systemically important risk-taking earlier and more effectively to prevent threats to financial stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-examine and tighten capital-reserve requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals call for a re-examination of capital-reserve requirements to make sure financial institutions have enough resources to make good on obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher or better-calibrated capital buffers are presented as a way to reduce insolvency risk and the need for government intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant government powers to take over and dismantle failing large institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration proposals would give the government new powers to take over and dismantle large institutions that fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having orderly resolution powers (instead of ad hoc bailouts) could allow failures like Lehman to be handled without systemic disruption, preventing moral hazard by not protecting creditors/management automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform executive compensation to discourage short-term risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration would order regulators to issue new executive compensation guidelines to ensure that companies don’t encourage short-term risk taking at the expense of long-term health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation rules aiming to align incentives with long-term firm health (vesting schedules, clawbacks, performance metrics) are presented as a tool to reduce managerial pursuit of short-term gains that increase systemic risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating an implicit safety net that advantages big firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Blume warns that proposals’ focus on averting problems with big institutions creates an implicit safety net and 'may provide a competitive advantage to some of the big firms at the expense of the little firms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should be designed to prevent competitive distortions where large firms take on more risk because they expect preferential treatment, and to avoid entrenching too-big-to-fail expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen shareholder oversight and board accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC has proposed strengthening shareholders’ hands: a non-binding 'say on pay' and making it easier for shareholders, mainly large ones, to field their own candidates for boards of directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While 'say on pay' may be of limited use, facilitating shareholder ability to nominate directors is supported as a means to improve director oversight and reduce cozy relationships that fail to constrain management risk-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address toxic/illiquid assets with credible resolution mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Government efforts to relieve banks of 'toxic assets' (using loans and guarantees to encourage private investors) have had little success; banks often prefer to keep illiquid assets and value them above market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective policies must account for bank incentives (they may delay loss recognition), and use mechanisms that lead to realistic pricing or compulsory resolution so that asset problems don’t inhibit lending indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit size, complexity, and interconnectedness of financial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Herring: 'Financial institutions that are too big to fail are simply too big. Financial institutions that are too complicated to fail are simply too complicated. Financial institutions that are too interconnected to fail are simply too interconnected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing size/complexity/interconnectedness or increasing oversight of such features is suggested to lower systemic risk and reduce the need for taxpayer-funded rescues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce overreliance on valuation models and credit ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Siegel faults management for 'taking false comfort in the triple-A ratings that Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s and Fitch gave' and notes mistaken faith in valuation models with too little track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers and firms should be wary of excessive reliance on opaque models and ratings; improve model validation, transparency, and independent oversight of rating practices to prevent misjudged risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance preventing excessive risk with avoiding insufficient credit availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that the main immediate problem may be insufficient risk-taking (tight credit): businesses and individuals are having a tough time getting loans even when creditworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory responses should strive for a balance—curbing reckless leverage while ensuring lending channels remain open so productive businesses can access capital for growth.
